sources.text:
Wall Street suffers historic losses as Dow, S&P 500 plunge into correction territory
Nvidia tumbled roughly 14%, and newly public Anthropic fell about 9% as Wall Street posted its worst week in months
U.S. stocks plunged Friday in one of Wall Street's worst trading sessions in years, when a massive sell-off in artificial intelligence companies wiped out the Nasdaq's gains for the year and pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory.
The historic sell-off sent major U.S. indexes sharply lower, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling nearly 950 points, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.28%.
Both the Dow and S&P 500 entered correction territory, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from their recent record highs.
The steep decline erased the Nasdaq's gains for the year, marking its second-largest single-day point drop on record.
ANTHROPIC'S $1.5 TRILLION IPO SETS OFF A FRESH WAVE OF TECH WEALTH HEADING FOR SOUTH FLORIDA
"It was a brutal day in the stock market with AI fears taking center stage," FOX Business anchor Gerri Willis reported Friday on "Special Report."
Investors directed much of their selling toward technology companies, putting additional pressure on the Nasdaq, Willis noted.
"Investors saved their real wrath for the tech-heavy Nasdaq," Willis said.
The massive sell-off came amid mounting concerns about the AI boom, with some of the industry's biggest names suffering steep losses, including chip-making giant Nvidia and newly public AI developer Anthropic.
HOLIDAY AIRFARES HIT HIGHEST LEVELS IN A DECADE AS JET FUEL PRICES SURGE
Nvidia shares tumbled approximately 14%, while Anthropic fell about 9% during its second trading session as a public company.
Friday's declines came despite strong earnings from Nvidia and a highly anticipated stock market debut for Anthropic, which failed to ease investor concerns about soaring AI valuations and spending.

sources.news_title: Nasdaq Erases 2026 Gain; Dow Jones, S&P 500 Slip Into Correction
sources.text:
U.S. stocks took a beating to close the trading week as the tech-fueled market rout intensified.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plummeted 1,261 points, or 5.28 percent, to 22,617 on Nov. 20. The Nasdaq posted a 10 percent weekly loss and is down nearly 3 percent this year, erasing all of its 2026 gains.
The S&P 500 tumbled 265 points, or 3.7 percent, to 6,910. The broad-market index fell 8.61 percent for the week and is up just 0.95 percent year to date.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average—a blue-chip index of 30 large publicly traded U.S. companies—declined 949 points, or 1.93 percent, to 48,147. The Dow fell 8 percent this week and is up marginally year to date: 0.17 percent.
Both the Dow and S&P 500 slipped into correction territory, meaning they are down at least 10 percent from their recent closing high.
The Russell 2000—an index of 2,000 small-cap companies—fell 73 points, or 2.76 percent, to 2,581. It also fell 7.48 percent for the week but remains up 4 percent year to date. The Russell is also in correction territory.
“Technical damage continues to mount,” Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial, told The Epoch Times in an emailed note.
Recent selloffs mirror the sharp declines seen at the onset of the pandemic in 2020 and the tariff tantrum in 2025.
Anthropic Enthusiasm Pauses
Despite its blockbuster debut on Wall Street, Anthropic failed to sustain momentum or lift the broader financial markets.
“Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO drew strong investor demand yesterday, but enthusiasm failed to spill over into the broader tech trade as peak AI cycle concerns lingered,” Turnquist said.
In its first full trading session, the Claude developer dropped 8.5 percent to less than $89.
“It has been a brutal week. There’s no way to sugarcoat it. Markets have a remarkable ability to humble even the most confident investors, and this week was a painful reminder that nobody has a crystal ball,” Stoyan Panayotov, founder and CEO of Babylon Wealth Management, said in a note shared with The Epoch Times.
No single event has driven the market lower. Instead, a perfect storm of factors fueled the selloff, said Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives.
The blue wave in this month’s midterm elections, Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia, the Anthropic initial public offering (IPO) marginally reducing liquidity, and a hawkish tone from the Federal Reserve have contributed to the ocean of red ink sweeping Wall Street.
“The $4 trillion AI buildout is still happening and our tech thesis into 2027 remains,” Ives said on X.
Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge—the CBOE Volatility Index—surged 26 percent to 35.89 to finish the trading week, its highest since late March.
Chipmaker Nvidia also tanked 14 percent to below $126—the lowest since May 2025—after Reuters reported the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating the company’s accounting.
President Donald Trump told reporters on Nov. 20 that Nvidia’s board should reinstate Huang, saying that his leadership is vital for the global artificial intelligence (AI) race and the U.S. economy.
“I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances,” Trump told reporters during a briefing at the White House. “That’s a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies.”
Nvidia’s board has confirmed that it does not intend to bring back the co-founder.
PCE Inflation in Focus
Next week will offer another update on the inflation picture.
The Federal Reserve’s go-to inflation measure—the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index—will be released on Nov. 25 for October’s numbers.
The consensus estimate suggests headline PCE will rise 0.3 percent month over month. Core PCE, which strips out the volatile energy and food components, is also expected to edge up 0.3 percent.
Looking ahead, Jamie Cox, managing partner at the Harris Financial Group, said investor sentiment will return to normal soon.
“At some point, the market will return to rationality and start paying attention to consumption and the positive effects for GDP,” Cox said in a note emailed to The Epoch Times.

sources.news_title: Has AI's honeymoon ended on Wall Street?
sources.text:
Although the AI industry has been the darling of Wall Street for years, the sector now makes investors wince as it reckons with a wave of concerns over dizzying spending and its promise to make the technology profitable.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index was indicative of this shift after plummeting 5.28 percent on Friday, wiping out all gains it had recorded since the start of the year.
"Markets were euphoric" about AI but "there's a huge repricing going on right now," Steve Sostick, a financial analyst with Interactive Brokers, told AFP.
The so-called "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks largely driving the market -- Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta and Tesla -- have seen their combined market capitalization fall by more than $4 trillion in the past month-and-a-half, according to an AFP analysis based on Bloomberg data -- a decrease larger than the annual GDP of France.
"You have a situation now where the bubble already deflated...The question now is how far down will it go?" Adam Sarhan, head of the financial platform MarketTerminal.com, told AFP in an interview.
- US midterms and Nvidia controversy -
While the trajectory of stock markets is never linear, the setbacks have piled up on tech darlings this month.
First, US midterm elections dominated by Democrats "really turned the tide, as it told us that American voters are not fans of artificial intelligence," Sostick said, referencing the many local ballot box measures restricting data centers.
Second, the biggest company in the semiconductor industry, Nvidia, has seen its longtime chief Jensen Huang resign over multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funneled restricted chips to that country.
With the chip market being so key to the AI industry, the disruption has had widespread ripple effects in the stock market.
- Looming debt -
"The AI investment boom has gone from a promising technology story to a capital markets extravaganza," said Stephen Innes, a manager at SPI Asset Management, with billions of dollars spent to develop the technology.
But as spending has ballooned, so has debt -- and profits have yet to match.
"As the capital needs grew, we started to see investors question how profitable all these investments might be, whether all this money was being spent wisely...the market hadn't been really asking these questions before," Sostick said.
"It seems absurd to ask people to invest money and not have a real sense of what's going to be the return on that investment," he added.
AI giant Anthropic, maker of Claude AI software, made its stock market debut Thursday, raking in an eye-watering $91 billion.
However, even with such a windfall, the company has acknowledged that its financing needs could require it to borrow money in the future.
"The opaqueness of AI-related debt is further compounded by circular links in the form of mutual commitments and interlinked ownerships between firms in the AI supply chain," the European Central Bank warned in a recent report.

US stocks: Wall Street ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
The three major indices closed much lower for the day
[NEW YORK] US stocks extended their rout on Friday (Nov 20), and the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally.
All three major US equity indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10 per cent below their record closing highs, confirming both indexes have entered a correction.
The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020.
The S&P 500 and the Dowlogged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling “liberation day” tariff package.
The Nasdaq’s weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index hasdipped into negative territory for the year.
“This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, appears to be accelerating to a certain degree,” said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana. “But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today.”
“Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time,” Northey added, referring to economic strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things.
Anthropic’s supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as US$2 trillion in market cap, failed to catch fire on Thursday, closing 17.1 per cent above its US$83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session.
In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic’s shares fell 9.1 per cent. Nvidia’s shares tumbled 13.8 per cent.
The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology.
“Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate earnings history; they did everything right,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. “A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t.”
The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has powered much of the broader stock market’s gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6 per cent in mid-June. That luster has faded, with the index’s year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7 per cent.
Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9%, while Meta dropped 5.9%.
Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1 per cent and its peer Nebius slid 16.1 per cent.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93 per cent, to 48,147.33, the S&P 500 lost 265.41 points, or 3.7 per cent, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28 per cent, to 22,617.73.
The CBOE Market Volatility Index, often referred to as Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” rose to its highest close since Apr 7, 2025.
Inflation, Fed in focus
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said the central bank’s policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels.
Markets are pricing a near-certain likelihood of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.
Next week’s personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed’s monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week.
Among other movers, Intuit shares fell 12.8 per cent after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about US$3.68 billion, five years after acquiring it for nearly three times as much.
UnitedHealth rose 2.8 per cent after TD Cowen upgraded its shares to a “buy” from a “hold” rating.
The AI selloff also sent Caterpillar 5 per cent lower on worries over weakening demand for its power-generating and backup power equipment.
Cryptocurrency firms including Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood tumbled between 6.3 per cent and 9.6 per cent after bitcoin dropped below the US$60,000 level.
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.77-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 38 new highs and 1,199 new lows on the NYSE.
On the Nasdaq, 928 stocks rose and 3,964 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 4.27-to-1 ratio.
The S&P 500 posted 3 new 52-week highs and 28 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 21 new highs and 826 new lows.
Volume on US exchanges was 25.19 billion shares, compared with the 19.50 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

Valentin Bogdanov: Has the AI bubble burst?. Not yet
Has the AI bubble burst?
Not yet. But it is no longer inflating — it is actively deflating.
There is a sharp sell-off in the American market today: Nasdaq 5%, Nvidia 12%, AMD 13%, Broadcom 13%, Micron Technology 14%, Nebius 15%.
In recent weeks, Nvidia has lost about $2 trillion in capitalization and has fallen by 30-47% from its October peaks. The shares are currently trading at about 13-15 profit margins, although revenue grew by +103% year-on-year in the last quarter. Huang left amid a scandal — and this increased the pressure. Chips, memory, and neoclouds are falling even more (to 37%/ 58%/ 63% of their highs).
This is not yet the collapse of the 2000 level (where the Nasdaq fell by ~80%, and a bunch of companies went to zero). Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, etc.) hold up better than pure-play AI infrastructure. The leaders' revenue is still growing very fast. Forrester recently set the green status in its "AI Bubble Model" (although it is already falling).
In China, the AI bubble has already burst before - the local tech index has lost about 40%. In prediction markets, the probability of a "bubble bursting before the end of 2026" has increased dramatically. At the same time, the technology is alive and continues to grow. It's just that the market has finally started asking when all this endless construction of data centers will begin to bring normal profits, and not just new rounds and debts.
Now it's still a strong correction, not a full-fledged crash. The question is how deep it will go.

S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as tech sell-off worsens - WSVN 7News | Miami News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 8.5%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 8.5% to $88.91, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Reuters reported a seventh consecutive S&P 500 decline and a 9.1% fall in Anthropic shares, one day after their market debut.
The AI selloff reaches the broader benchmarks
Friday’s losses followed earlier pressure on the same trade. The FINANCIAL’s November 5 coveragedescribed selling in chipmakers and businesses tied to data-center construction as investors reassessed AI spending and potential regulatory scrutiny. That report used intraday readings from the earlier session; Friday’s figures reflect a later, completed trading day.
The Nasdaq’s own index page also showed a November 20 reading of 22,617.73 and a decline of 5.28%, the more precise percentage behind the rounded 5.3% figure. The Composite covers domestic and international common-type stocks listed on Nasdaq, giving it a different membership base from a U.S.-only index.
Anthropic closes its offering during the market retreat
Anthropic said Friday that it had completed its initial public offering of 1.127 billion Class A shares at $83 each. The total included underwriters’ full exercise of an option to purchase an additional 147 million shares. Its shares began trading Thursday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.
The company put gross proceeds from the offering at approximately $93.5 billion, before underwriting discounts, commissions and other expenses. Of that amount, about $91.6 billion went to Anthropic. The offering also included shares sold by existing stockholders, from whose sales the company received no proceeds.
Anthropic separately announced the closing of a concurrent private placement worth approximately $26 billion. Buyers included Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC Partners. The Class N shares in that placement were sold at the same $83 price used for the public offering.
The company reported combined gross proceeds of about $119.5 billion from the public offering, including selling stockholders’ shares, and the private placement. Those fundraising figures describe the transactions at their offering price, before expenses; they do not represent the stock’s value in subsequent exchange trading.
Nvidia faces a reported accounting inquiry
In a separate Friday report, Reuters said SEC enforcement staff were examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia, citing two people briefed on the matter who spoke anonymously. The SEC declined to comment and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters. The news agency could not establish the inquiry’s start date or precise accounting questions. An investigation does not establish wrongdoing.
Earlier in the week, Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and 20% from the preceding quarter. The fiscal quarter ended October 25. Data-center revenue reached $107.6 billion, increasing 110% from a year earlier, according to its November 17 release.
Nvidia reported a gross margin of 74.8% under generally accepted accounting principles and diluted earnings of $2.70 a share. Its fourth-quarter outlook called for revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, and gross margins between 71% and 72%. The company said that forecast included an additional week in the quarter.
The outlook assumed no data-center compute revenue from China. Nvidia also reported returning $28.1 billion to shareholders through repurchases and cash dividends during the third quarter, with approximately $227.3 billion remaining under its repurchase authorization at quarter-end. These were company-reported results and plans released before Friday’s trading session.
The quarterly results also showed GAAP operating income of $77.5 billion, up 115% from a year earlier, and net income of $65.3 billion, up 105%. Operating expenses totaled $9.2 billion, a 57% increase from the comparable year-earlier period.

Intuit’s November 19 results announcement combined an updated revenue forecast with an agreement to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion. The proposed consideration comprised $3.31 billion in cash and $368 million in Bending Spoons stock.
The transaction is expected to close in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions. Intuit said its guidance excluded any impact from the pending sale and would be updated when the transaction closed. It intends to use cash proceeds to repurchase shares during fiscal 2027.
The company forecast full-year revenue of $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion, representing growth of 8% to 9%. It attributed its updated revenue guidance to Credit Karma, with corresponding changes to consumer-segment and companywide projections. Intuit reiterated its full-year operating-income and earnings-per-share guidance.

The Federal Reserve released minutes Wednesday of its October 27–28 policy meeting. The document records October discussions, preceding Friday’s closing market levels and this week’s corporate announcements.

A majority noted tighter financial conditions since the September meeting, citing higher mortgage rates and wider credit spreads for some higher-risk and AI-related borrowers. Many observed that higher borrowing costs and more selective lending had weighed on housing, commercial real estate and small businesses.
Volatility measures and the holiday calendar
The Cboe VIX index measures expected stock-market volatility over the coming 30 days using prices of S&P 500 options. Its construction therefore differs from the Nasdaq Composite, which measures share prices. Cboe describes VIX as reflecting market expectations derived from option prices.

The exchange’s normal core session runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern. Its published Thanksgiving schedule applies to a shorter session the day after the holiday. That calendar sets the available regular trading hours following the week’s losses.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 22,617.73. Nasdaq’s index page displayed a 5.28% decline, equivalent to 5.3% when rounded to one decimal place.

A correction conventionally means a decline of at least 10% from a recent market high.

sources.text:
The S&P 500 fell into a correction Friday, and the Nasdaq Composite gave back everything it had gained in 2026.
The S&P 500 closed more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record close, and the Dow also ended in correction territory. The S&P fell 3.59% to 6,918.45, its seventh straight losing session and its longest losing streak since February 2020.
Investors were “panic selling” as they tried to judge whether enthusiasm for AI had peaked, Benedicte Lowe, an equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas, told CNBC.
Anthropic led the AI slide, as Fortune reported Friday morning. The Claude maker raised $81.34 billion in an IPO that valued it at $1.414 trillion, and its shares fell about 9% Friday, their second day of trading, giving back much of Thursday’s 17% pop. Reuters cited worries about slower data-center expansion, higher borrowing costs and Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
The people with the most money in stocks already felt it. Those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances in the University of Michigan’s November survey, which ran through Nov. 16, “consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets,” survey director Joanne Hsu said.
What the panic looked like
Chipmakers took the worst of it. Micron, hotlink]Broadcom[/hotlink], Nvidia, and AMD were down between roughly 12% and 14%. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, topped 30 for the first time since March, CNBC reported.
The selling wasn’t only in the U.S. Taiwan’s stock index fell 5.65% Friday, capping its steepest weekly drop since October 1997, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC. Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell about 5%.
Washington added to it. President Donald Trump threatened a “tremendous tax” on U.S. companies that build data centers abroad, CNBC reported.
At midday, some analysts still saw a rotation.
“Money is leaving tech, not the market,” independent tech analyst Luke Lango, editor of the Innovation Investor newsletter, wrote in a note at 12:59 p.m. He said the Dow and the equal-weight S&P were higher at the time. His advice: Avoid AI stocks “while they’re being combative teenagers.” He also pointed to credit: SpaceX had to raise the yield on its $32 billion debt sale to 8.3%, which he read as the “capital spigot” closing for weaker AI borrowers such as CoreWeave and Nebius.
The calm-down chorus
Most of the Street said the drop would pass.
“Given the solid economic and fundamental backdrop, the move appears to be highly sentiment driven,” Chris Larkin, head of trading at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley, said in commentary sent to Fortune. He added that “only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983” turned into bear markets.
Deutsche Bank’s Binky Chadha called the market “very oversold” and said growth and earnings remained strong, according to CNBC. JPMorgan Asset Management chief global strategist David Kelly told Seeking Alpha markets were overdue for a tech correction. Chuck Carlson, CEO of Horizon Investment Services, told Reuters the market may be in a correction within a bull market.
E*Trade’s own research is less soothing. A March 2025 E*TRADE study of the 14 times since 1983 that the S&P 500 first closed 10% or more below a record found five became bear markets. But the index fell another 10% or more after closing in correction six of those 14 times, and in 1990 and 1998 it came within a point of bear territory. The median total drop from the record was 19.9%.
The backdrop Larkin calls solid includes a rate hike on the way. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday the central bank will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high, Reuters reported. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, per CME FedWatch, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.
The Fed meets Dec. 9. Investors will find out then whether Friday was panic or just early.

All three major U.S. stock indexes ended sharply lower. The S&P 500 and Dow closed more than 10% below their record closing highs, confirming that both had entered a correction.

He noted that investor sentiment was currently outweighing underlying economic fundamentals, including economic strength and solid corporate earnings.
Anthropic Debut Fails to Restore AI Investor Confidence
Investors had hoped Anthropic’s highly anticipated public listing would help restore confidence in the AI sector. Instead, the company’s debut failed to generate sustained enthusiasm.
Anthropic shares closed 17.1% above their $83 offering price on Thursday, but enthusiasm weakened throughout the session. The stock suffered a steep decline during its second trading day.
The public offering, combined with Nvidia’s latest quarterly earnings report, did little to ease concerns about the risks associated with artificial intelligence and the enormous spending required to develop the technology.
Nvidia delivered an exceptionally strong quarterly performance, but investors remained unconvinced that its results could resolve broader concerns about AI valuations and long-term profitability.
“A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which has helped drive much of the broader market’s gains in recent months, has also lost momentum. After rising 106.6% year-to-date in mid-June, its earlier gains have faded considerably.
Big Tech and AI Infrastructure Stocks Slide
The selloff spread across major technology companies and businesses connected to AI infrastructure.
Amazon and Meta recorded steep declines, while cloud computing firms CoreWeave and Nebius also suffered significant losses.
The weakness reflects growing investor concerns about the enormous capital requirements of AI development and whether companies can generate sufficient returns to justify their spending.
As technology stocks came under pressure, investors shifted toward more defensive areas of the market, including consumer staples and healthcare.
This rotation suggests that investors are becoming more cautious about high-growth technology companies while seeking greater stability elsewhere.
Federal Reserve Rate Outlook Adds to Market Pressure
Inflation and monetary policy remained important concerns for investors.

Markets were pricing in a near-certain probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate increase at the Federal Reserve’s next meeting in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.

Individual Stocks Move on Company-Specific Developments
Several companies also experienced notable share-price movements.

UnitedHealth shares moved higher after TD Cowen upgraded its rating to “buy” from “hold.”
Caterpillar shares declined amid concerns that weakening demand could affect sales of its power-generation and backup-power equipment.
The cryptocurrency downturn added further pressure to related stocks. Bitcoin fell below $60,000, weighing on Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood.
Major U.S. Indexes Record Sharp Losses

With major indexes now in correction territory, investors face a more challenging environment as they weigh corporate earnings, technology valuations, inflation and the possibility of further Federal Reserve tightening.

sources.news_title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as rout in tech stocks tanks the market
sources.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 8.5%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.2%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 14% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 30%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 8.5% to $88.91, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, several companies managed to gain ground despite strong downward pressure on the market. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.
An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported the closing price and percentage change for Anthropic shares.

A major source of investor anxiety involves proposed changes to oversight of Medicare Advantage, the privately administered alternative to traditional Medicare.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has proposed tighter measures targeting potentially improper payments and questionable diagnosis coding practices.
One area of concern is known as upcoding, in which diagnosis information can make patients appear more medically complex, potentially increasing payments to insurers under Medicare Advantage’s risk-adjustment system.
Federal officials have sought stronger oversight of these practices, while insurers face uncertainty about how expanded auditing and enforcement could affect future revenue.
For companies such as UnitedHealth, Humana, and CVS Health’s Aetna division, changes to reimbursement rules and compliance requirements could influence profitability.
The market reaction reflects concern about the potential financial implications of regulatory changes, not a final determination that the proposed measures will be implemented in their current form.
Bernie Sanders’ Medicare Proposal Creates Additional Uncertainty
Healthcare shares are also responding to renewed debate over federal healthcare policy.
Sen. Bernie Sanders has advanced a Medicare expansion proposal that includes lowering the eligibility age from 65 to 55 and broadening coverage for services such as dental, hearing, and vision care.
Such changes could affect the competitive landscape for private health insurers and alter expectations for future government reimbursement.
However, financial analysts have emphasized that major legislative changes would face substantial political and procedural obstacles.
The proposal has not become law, and the precise effects on insurers and hospital operators would depend on the final legislation, reimbursement structures, and implementation requirements.
For investors, the immediate concern is uncertainty surrounding the sector’s regulatory outlook rather than a confirmed change in federal healthcare benefits.
Why Hospital Stocks Are Falling Alongside Insurance Companies
Hospital operators face a different set of financial pressures from health insurers, but the two industries are closely connected.
Hospitals depend on payments from private insurance companies, Medicare, Medicaid, and patients.
Changes to government coverage programs, payment rates, or insurance participation can affect hospital revenue and operating margins.
Investors are therefore reassessing how potential healthcare policy changes could influence reimbursement levels and patient coverage.
Community Health Systems’ steep five-day decline demonstrates the market’s sensitivity to these uncertainties.
However, not every healthcare company has the same business model or exposure to federal insurance programs. The sector’s recent losses should not be interpreted as evidence that all healthcare businesses face identical financial risks.
What the Market Decline Means for LGBTQ Businesses and Investors
For LGBTQ-owned businesses, entrepreneurs, and investors, the broader market retreat highlights the importance of understanding how financial-market volatility can affect business operations.
Small and independently owned companies may encounter tighter lending conditions, changing consumer confidence, and increased uncertainty when planning expansion or capital expenditures.
Businesses connected to healthcare, employee benefits, and insurance services may also need to monitor proposed changes to federal reimbursement and coverage policies.
For LGBTQ individuals and families, developments involving Medicare and private health insurance may carry additional implications for healthcare access and financial planning.
However, declining insurance-company share prices do not automatically mean that patient coverage or existing healthcare benefits have changed.
Business owners should distinguish between market reactions to proposed policies and actual regulatory or legislative changes.
Wall Street Faces a Critical Test as November Selloff Continues
The latest market turbulence illustrates the interconnected pressures affecting U.S. equities.
Technology investors are reassessing artificial intelligence valuations, while healthcare investors are confronting uncertainty surrounding federal oversight and reimbursement policy.
Even sectors traditionally viewed as defensive have struggled to provide consistent protection during the recent selloff.
Friday’s developing session will help determine whether the Nasdaq’s move into negative year-to-date territory persists through the closing bell and whether broader indexes can stabilize after several consecutive declines.
For now, Wall Street’s November downturn serves as a reminder that defensive investment strategies can reduce certain risks without eliminating exposure to market volatility.

S&P 500 and Dow enter correction territory, Nasdaq loses 2026 gains as Anthropic dives
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Major stock indexes entered correction territory on Friday while the Nasdaq wiped out all its 2026 gains to end a brutal trading week following Anthropic’s IPO.
The S&P 500 fell 3.7% and the Dow slipped 1.9%, or 949 points – tipping both into correction territory, or down more than 10% from recent closing records.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq plummeted 5.3% and was down 2.7% so far this year.
Advertisement
Anthropic’s market debut on the Nasdaq Thursday initially seemed like a boon to Wall Street, raising $81 billion for the AI giant and beating out Elon Musk’s SpaceX as the largest-ever IPO.
But the stock fell 8.5% Friday, wiping out most of its 17% jump from the day before and nearing Facebook’s dramatic dive after its 2012 IPO.
Though it’s not unusual for companies to see their shares jump and then decline after they start trading in US markets, Anthropic’s drop far exceeds the two-day declines of recent predecessors like SpaceX, SK Hynix and Alibaba.
Advertisement
It comes amid mounting anxiety around the AI trade, as investors fear a pause on data center projects due to Democrats’ sweep of the midterms; the future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang; and potential regulatory hurdles as officials look to clamp down on Chinese export controls.
“I think investors are taking a harder look at how much companies are spending on AI and how soon that spending will pay off. Anthropic’s reversal after its IPO adds to that unease, and when stocks as big as Nvidia sell off, you feel it across the market,” Mark White, advisor at Mark White Wealth Advisors, told The Post.
“You can be right about AI changing the economy and still pay too much for an AI stock. When a stock is priced for years of strong growth, even a small change in expectations can produce a big drop,” he added.
Advertisement
Dan Ives, partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co, said it seems like more of a “panic-driven sell-off” caused by the “perfect storm” of AI concerns – not a warning bell reminiscent of the “dot-com bubble” of the early 2000s or the 2008 financial crisis.
Investors were hopeful Anthropic’s IPO and strong earnings from Nvidia — even after Huang was forced out for having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy — would help revive the AI trade.
But traders are increasingly concerned that Dems could halt data-center construction, possibly stifling revenue at AI firms, and that the Nvidia scandal is inviting scrutiny of the industry.
While SpaceX saw a record showing in June, the company entered the market at a much more optimistic time. It also owns a rocket-launch firm and satellite business, while Anthropic is purely an AI play, known for its chatbot Claude and Claude Code tool.
Advertisement
Chipmakers including Micron, Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia all slipped more than 13% on Friday.
The Commerce Department has already moved to close a loophole that China was using to skirt around export controls on American chips as it faces backlash following the Nvidia honeypot scandal.
It approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, according to the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
That came after Huang reportedly lobbied President Trump for the ability to export chips to China while he was in a years-long relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, a Singapore-based executive and suspected Chinese spy.
Advertisement
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for the mess, claiming Lutnick failed to block such exports even though he was aware of a government memo linking Huang’s mistress to the Chinese government.
Huang and Lutnick have both agreed to testify before Congress.
AMD has also been caught in the crossfire, after a short seller on Thursday alleged the company “has its own China problem.”
Hunterbrook Media claimed in a report that “after the US blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers.”

It also said stricter export controls from Washington could slam AMD, alleging the firm “bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong” and “depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips.”

US stocks slide as AI sell-off intensifies; S&P 500 approaches correction
sources.text:
Wall Street's sell-off deepened on Friday as a sharp decline in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks dragged the S&P 500 close to correction territory and put the benchmark index on course for its biggest weekly loss in months.
The S&P 500 fell around 2%, leaving it about 10% below its record high of October 6. A closing decline of more than 10% from that peak would put the index in what investors call a “correction”. The index was also on track to post its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 3.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 12:20 pm Eastern time.
Despite gains in a larger number of S&P 500 stocks, losses among major technology companies weighed heavily on the index because of their large market valuations. AI-linked stocks, which had driven much of Wall Street's gains this year, were now leading the decline.
Investors have grown concerned that the high valuations of AI companies may not be justified by their earnings prospects and that their heavy spending on the technology could take time to generate returns. 
Fears of a bubble in the sector have added to the pressure.
The sell-off also comes amid a shift in political power following the midterm elections, in which the Republican Party, widely seen as more supportive of the technology industry, suffered an electoral setback.
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, also came under pressure in its market debut. Its shares fell 12.4% to $85.16 on Friday, although they remained above the initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.
The company's listing was the biggest public stock offering on record, with its valuation briefly crossing $2 trillion. However, its shares joined the broader technology sell-off on Friday.
Newly listed technology companies often see sharp price swings in the days following their market debut. SpaceX, which previously held the record for the biggest IPO, gained nearly 50% in its first three trading days before falling below its IPO price a month later.
Chipmakers, which have benefited from rising investment in AI data centres, were among the biggest losers, the Associated Press reported.
Nvidia fell 7.4%, marking its ninth decline in the past 10 trading sessions. The company also faced pressure amid concerns about its future following the reported sudden downfall of its former CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang.
Advanced Micro Devices dropped 11.7%, while Broadcom declined 11.5%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index slid 9%.
Outside the technology sector, however, several stocks advanced. General Mills, the maker of Cheerios, rose 4.8%, while homebuilder Lennar gained 3.4%.
In the bond market, US Treasury yields fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 4.93% from 5.04% late on Thursday.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, declined 0.3% to $91.69 a barrel despite continuing tensions near the Strait of Hormuz amid the US war with Iran.

S&P 500 falls 10% from record, entering correction as AI trade unravels
-   Share via
A bruising tech rout roiled global markets, driving U.S. stocks toward their longest slide since 2020 as investors piled into bonds.
The unraveling of the artificial-intelligence trade spurred a rush from risk, driving the S&P 500 down 10% from its peak, matching the definition of a technical correction. The Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5%. Anthropic PBC’s 11% plunge on its second day of trading is emblematic of the turn in sentiment.
The resurgence in volatility spurred demand for defensive shares and haven assets including Treasuries. The dollar headed for a fourth straight weekly gain. Emerging-market shares extended a drop from a record to 20%.
Anthropic’s debut consumed the attention of investors, with stocks along the supply chain moving on even minor developments around the deal’s size or pricing. Now that the IPO is wrapped up, that exuberance is giving way to mounting doubts over the durability of the AI trade.
“Another perceived risk-clearing event failed to revive risk appetite,” said Adam Turnquist at LPL Financial. “Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO drew strong investor demand yesterday, but enthusiasm failed to spill over into the broader tech trade as peak AI cycle concerns lingered.”
Questions remain over whether the vast spending on the AI buildout can be sustained as regulation looks set to tighten and the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise rates.
As investors fret over tech valuations, geopolitical turmoil and rates, chart watchers are looking for clues on whether the worst of the rout is over. The U.S. equity benchmark this week broke below its 200-day moving average, and is now near a major structural floor between a rebound and a deeper year-end pullback.
“Technical damage is mounting,” said Adam Turnquist at LPL Financial. “Stability in the AI trade and the S&P 500 holding key support near 7,000 will be important factors for a durable recovery.”
Stocks are likely biased to the downside over the very near-term until technical indicators are washed out, said Chris Senyek at Wolfe Research. Absent an Iran peace deal, concerns over the impact of inflation of Fed policy and AI worries remain key overhangs for equities, he noted.
“A capitulatory washout could ultimately prove constructive,” said Mark Hackett at Nationwide. “If this evolves into a true flush, it may serve as the reset needed to improve positioning, sentiment, and the odds of a more sustainable rally into year-end.”
Nazareth writes for Bloomberg.

The US tech sell-off rapidly accelerated on Friday as fears over the AI sector spreading across all major indexes, with newly public Anthropic plummeted more than 9 per cent.
Worries that Wall Street’s biggest investment boom in decades is fizzling out drove the US equity benchmark to its longest slide since 2020, with the gauge down 3.5 per cent.
The Nasdaq 100 lost 5.61 per cent, adding to its longest losing streak since 2020. Nvidia dropped 13.8 per cent as Reuters reported that US regulators are investigating its accounting practices.
The past month has seen Nvidia lose more than 40 per cent of its value, after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a businesswoman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services.
Anthropic opened to huge fanfare on Thursday, reaching about $105 per share, but it has steadily declined since then. Other tech stocks were rocked, including Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet, all of which ended a brutal week in the red.
“Smackdown!” said Steve Sosnick at Interactive Brokers. “The problem stems from investors’ rapidly changed perceptions about technology, particularly the pace and cost of the artificial-intelligence buildout.”
Richard Saperstein at Treasury Partners said the stock market is going through an AI repricing, "reflecting an environment of slowing data centre buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth".
The gloom is dragging other indexes down, too, with the S&P 500 losing 3.7 per cent on Friday while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.93 per cent.
“We are in the midst of a garden-variety correction, with the market’s leadership moving around,” said Gaurav Mallik at Modera Wealth Management.
“While we expect technology to recover and perform well, it may cede its leadership to other sectors like industrials and financials and more value-orientated areas of the market.”

The resurgence in volatility spurred demand for defensive shares and haven assets including Treasuries. The US dollar ended with a fourth consecutive weekly gain. Emerging markets were on the cusp of a bear market.
Anthropic’s debut consumed the attention of investors, with stocks along the supply chain moving on even minor developments around the deal’s size or pricing. Now that the IPO is wrapped up, that exuberance is giving way to mounting doubts over the durability of the AI trade.

sources.text:
From Nvidia To Amazon, Tech Giants Face Stunning Reversal As Nasdaq Erases 2026 Gains
Technology shares led a broad market retreat as investors questioned lofty AI valuations and responded to rising expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike.
U.S. stocks plunged Friday as a deepening sell-off in artificial intelligence companies sent Wall Street toward its worst weekly performance in more than a year, with investors increasingly concerned about technology valuations and the prospect of higher interest rates.
The Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 5% in late afternoon trading, erasing its gains for 2026. The S&P 500 dropped 3.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.7%. Both the Dow and S&P 500 slipped into correction territory, trading more than 10% below their October record highs.
The S&P 500 was on track for its seventh consecutive losing session, marking its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic rattled global financial markets.
All three major indexes were headed toward their worst weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when President Donald Trump's sweeping tariff announcement triggered a global market downturn. The Dow had already lost approximately 6.2% this week through Thursday's close.
Technology stocks were at the center of Friday's retreat, as the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence developer Anthropic failed to restore confidence in a sector that had powered much of Wall Street's rally this year.
The company behind the Claude chatbot raised approximately $81 billion in its initial public offering on Thursday, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in history. Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and initially surged more than 30% when trading began. However, the stock surrendered much of those gains before Thursday's closing bell and continued falling Friday.
The disappointing performance compounded concerns about whether the enormous amounts of money flowing into AI companies and infrastructure can generate sufficient returns to justify their valuations.
Semiconductor manufacturers suffered some of Friday's heaviest losses. Nvidia shares plunged approximately 12%, while Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Micron Technology also recorded double-digit declines during the session.
Amazon and Meta Platforms also came under pressure, while AI cloud infrastructure providers CoreWeave and Nebius recorded substantial losses. Companies benefiting indirectly from the expansion of AI infrastructure were also affected. Caterpillar shares declined amid concerns that a slowdown in data center investment could weaken demand for power generation equipment.
The technology rout spread internationally, with Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi both falling more than 5%. Adding to Wall Street's challenges were growing expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again as inflation remains stubbornly elevated.
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook indicated Friday that monetary policy was not sufficiently restrictive to address current inflation levels. Financial markets were pricing in a more than 95% probability of an interest rate increase at the central bank's December meeting.
Higher interest rates generally put pressure on growth stocks because they reduce the present value of anticipated future earnings and make financing more expensive. Technology companies pursuing capital-intensive AI expansion projects are particularly exposed to those conditions.
Elsewhere, Intuit shares plunged after the financial software company lowered its annual revenue growth forecast and announced an agreement to sell its Mailchimp business for approximately $3.7 billion.

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”

Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

NEW YORK: Investors on Wednesday (Nov 18) were absorbing a blockbuster earnings report from chip titan Nvidia and getting set for the long-awaited IPO from AI giant Anthropic, though stocks fell across the board as uncertainty continues to stalk the industry.
The technology sector faces questions over whether huge AI investments will ever pay off, and has now been rocked by claims that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy - who might have funnelled restricted chips to Beijing.
The scandal, along with reports that Huang had affairs with Nvidia employees, led to his resignation as chief executive last week, raising doubts about the prospects for one of the world's largest companies.
In its highly anticipated earnings release Tuesday, Nvidia said third-quarter revenue doubled to more than US$115 billion, generating a net profit of US$65.3 billion.
The firm also increased its forecast for next year's revenue to 75 per cent growth.
But investors also noted that the United States moved to tighten restrictions on Chinese access to chips, while Huang has agreed to meet US lawmakers on Dec 1 to answer questions about national security concerns.
"For Nvidia, strong earnings have bought management time," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.
"For the broader AI trade, they reinforce confidence in infrastructure demand, but the next leg of the rally may depend increasingly on which companies can turn that demand into sustainable profits."
Interim CEO Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" after the loss of Huang, a pivotal player in the eye-watering growth of the artificial intelligence industry.
But the US markets were unforgiving for Nvidia, whose shares fell by 2.9 per cent by the close in New York, continuing a run of weeks of heavy losses and in keeping with a slump across two of the three main US indexes on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq the only one to close in the green.
European bourses also slipped into the red by close of play, as did most markets in Asia.
Analysts noted that many investors were likely reducing their holdings in other stocks to free up funds to buy shares in Anthropic.
"Investors are preparing for a blowout IPO tomorrow from Anthropic," said Peter Cardillo from Spartan Capital Securities. "Hopefully (it) might begin to alleviate some of the worries that the market is undergoing."
The five-year-old startup is going public Thursday in an IPO that could raise US$65 billion or more - giving investors a first chance to bet directly on a stand-alone AI giant in a test of how long the sector's spending boom can last.
"The issue is over six times subscribed, and there's plenty of excitement ahead of the first public offering of a pure frontier lab at the forefront of AI development," said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.
Anthropic is widely seen as the leader for AI products, while Nvidia has been dubbed the "central bank" of the industry for its investments in start-ups and providing backstops on loans.
On currency markets, the dollar extended its recent gains against major rivals on expectations the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and possibly again early next year.
That could slow economic growth, but it would raise returns on US government bonds, considered one of the safest investments available.
On Wednesday, minutes from the Fed's last meeting in October showed that "almost all" policymaker expected further hikes to be necessary, with Governor Chris Waller telling US broadcaster CNBC he could back a 50-basis-point increase.

Why Financial Markets Had the Worst Day of the Year (And How Apple Did)

Why Financial Markets Had the Worst Day of the Year (And How Apple Did)
Toggle Dark Mode
On Friday, November 20, 2026, global markets suffered one of their sharpest single-day drops of the year. The S&P 500 fell roughly 3.7%, the Nasdaq Composite sank about 5.3% (wiping out its 2026 gains), and the Dow declined nearly 2%. Both the S&P 500 and Dow entered correction territory, more than 10% below their October highs. The S&P logged a seventh straight losing session. Overall, the week ranked among the worst in years. Trillions in market value vanished worldwide, with Asia recording its weakest performance since 2020.
The damage was concentrated in the AI and semiconductor names that had driven most of 2026’s gains. Apple was not immune: AAPL closed near $343, down about 1.8% on the day and off its recent peak near $361.
Multiple Forces Hit at Once
The sell-off reflected a convergence of concerns rather than a single trigger.
AI Return Doubts
Investors questioned whether the massive spending on data centers, chips, and infrastructure would deliver sufficient returns. Anthropic’s record IPO—the largest ever—failed to restore confidence. The stock faded after a strong open and continued lower on Friday, highlighting worries about profitability and circular financing across the sector.
Nvidia Leadership Shock
Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO amid personal scandals and national-security questions removed a central figure who had underwritten much of the AI buildout. Regulatory scrutiny on chip exports added further uncertainty.
Political and Rate Pressures
Democratic gains in the midterms raised the prospect of tighter data-center rules. At the same time, sticky inflation kept markets focused on the possibility of further Federal Reserve rate hikes, raising the cost of the long-duration capital projects that underpin the AI boom.
Year-end Portfolio Rebalancing and Profit-taking
These fundamental worries landed during a period when many institutional portfolios and funds systematically rebalance. After a strong run in technology and AI-related stocks through most of 2026, large asset managers, pension funds, endowments, and mutual funds that maintain fixed target allocations (for example, a set percentage in equities versus bonds, or within equities a cap on any single sector or theme) needed to trim winners. Selling high-flying tech and AI names to lock in gains and restore target weights is a routine year-end process. When that mechanical selling coincides with already fragile sentiment, it can accelerate and deepen a decline. Hedge funds and other active managers facing performance pressure or redemptions often amplify the move by reducing exposure at the same time.
The combination turned what might have been a modest pullback into a more pronounced rout. Defensive sectors and bonds attracted inflows as investors raised cash and rotated away from the prior year’s winners.
Implications for Apple
Apple’s decline was milder than that of pure-play AI and semiconductor stocks because the company is less dependent on external data-center spending and maintains a more diversified revenue base. Still, broad risk-off flows and profit-taking in mega-cap technology hit AAPL along with the rest of the sector. Apple Intelligence features, services growth, and the installed base remain intact, but this week shows how even relatively resilient names can be swept along when funds systematically reduce tech exposure at year-end.
For longer-term holders, the rebalancing dynamic is familiar: strong performers are often trimmed into year-end, creating short-term pressure that does not necessarily alter the underlying business outlook. Apple’s balance sheet, cash generation, and product cycle continue to provide a degree of insulation relative to more speculative AI infrastructure plays.
Markets can stabilize once forced and mechanical selling runs its course, particularly if inflation data or Fed commentary eases rate-hike fears. For now, the November 20 session illustrated how narrative concerns, leadership uncertainty, and the calendar-driven habit of taking profits after a strong year can reinforce one another. iDrop News will keep tracking the effects on Apple and the wider technology sector.

sources.news_title: THE CLOSING BELL: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
sources.text:
By DAMIAN J. TROISE and ALEX VEIGA AP Business Writers
NEW YORK (AP) — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
___
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

Introduction: A Brutal End to the Week for U.S. and Canadian Stocks
Wall Street suffered another severe selloff on Friday, November 20, 2026, as concerns about artificial intelligence valuations, financing, and the sustainability of the AI investment boom intensified.
The Nasdaq Composite plunged nearly 5.3%, suffering the steepest decline among the major U.S. indexes and finishing in negative territory for the year.
The S&P 500 fell 3.6%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 1.9%.
According to the day’s market reporting, both the Dow and S&P 500 finished in correction territory, meaning they had declined more than 10% from their previous highs.
Canada’s stock market also suffered substantial losses.
The S&P/TSX Composite plunged 838.88 points, or 2.47%, closing at 33,189.85.
The selling was particularly severe among semiconductor companies. Nvidia shares reportedly fell 14%, while AMD, Broadcom, and Micron experienced double-digit declines.
Meanwhile, Anthropic shares dropped 8% in their second trading session following a record-setting IPO.
Gold prices declined nearly 4%, and bitcoin fell below $59,000.
The central story of November 20: Investors are no longer simply questioning whether artificial intelligence will transform the economy. They are questioning whether the enormous valuations and investments associated with AI can be financially justified.
