The Dow also fell, extending its retreat from previous highs.
What does correction territory mean?
A stock-market correction is commonly defined as a decline of at least 10% from a recent peak.
Corrections are a normal, although uncomfortable, feature of investing.
They can occur because of changes in economic expectations, interest rates, corporate earnings, or investor sentiment.
A correction does not necessarily lead to a bear market.
However, it indicates that investors have significantly reduced their expectations for stock prices.
2. Nvidia Plunges 14% as Semiconductor Stocks Lead the Selloff
Nvidia, one of the most influential companies in the artificial intelligence industry, reportedly fell 14% on Friday.
The decline came despite the company’s stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings earlier in the week.
Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion and earnings per share of $2.68, both exceeding analysts’ forecasts.
It also issued an optimistic fourth-quarter outlook and announced a $150 billion share repurchase program.
Yet investors continued selling the stock. The market needs Jensen Huang back.
Why would Nvidia fall after strong earnings?
The answer lies in the distinction between business performance and investor expectations.
Nvidia’s financial results demonstrate substantial demand for AI computing technology.
However, its valuation depends on expectations for future growth.
If investors become less confident that AI spending will continue expanding at the same pace, they may reduce the price they are willing to pay for the company’s shares.
The danger of high expectations
A company can deliver exceptional financial performance and still become a disappointing investment if its stock was purchased at an excessive valuation.
Nvidia’s decline illustrates that even the strongest businesses are not immune to changes in market sentiment.
The question facing investors is whether the current selloff represents a temporary adjustment or a more fundamental reassessment of the AI industry’s future profitability.
3. AMD, Broadcom, and Micron Suffer Double-Digit Declines
Nvidia was not alone.
According to the supplied report, AMD, Broadcom, and Micron Technology also suffered double-digit stock-price declines Friday.
These companies operate in different parts of the semiconductor industry, but all have exposure to artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.
AMD
Advanced Micro Devices competes in markets for processors used in computers, servers, and AI systems.
Investors have been optimistic about the company’s opportunities in AI computing.
However, expectations for rapid growth also create valuation risks.
Broadcom
Broadcom supplies semiconductor and networking technologies used in data centers and communications infrastructure.
Its exposure to AI-related spending has attracted considerable investor interest.
Nevertheless, the company remains sensitive to changes in expectations for technology investment.
Micron Technology
Micron manufactures memory products used in computers, data centers, and AI systems.
Demand for high-performance memory has increased alongside the growth of AI computing.
However, the memory industry has historically experienced periods of strong growth followed by downturns.
Why the entire sector is falling
The simultaneous decline of several major semiconductor companies suggests that investors are reassessing the broader AI infrastructure investment thesis.
This is different from a selloff caused by disappointing earnings at a single company.
It indicates concern about the industry as a whole.
4. The Nasdaq-100 Reveals Even More Severe Damage
One of Friday’s most striking statistics concerned the Nasdaq-100.
According to the supplied reporting, 71 of the index’s 101 reported constituents were already in bear-market territory.
That means their share prices had declined at least 20% from their respective peaks.
The report also stated that all 20 semiconductor and memory-chip stocks in the index were in bear-market territory.

The S&P 500 fell into a correction Friday, and the Nasdaq Composite gave back everything it had gained in 2026.
The S&P 500 closed more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record close, and the Dow also ended in correction territory. The S&P fell 3.59% to 6,918.45, its seventh straight losing session and its longest losing streak since February 2020.
Investors were “panic selling” as they tried to judge whether enthusiasm for AI had peaked, Benedicte Lowe, an equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas, told CNBC.
Anthropic led the AI slide, as Fortune reported Friday morning. The Claude maker raised $81.34 billion in an IPO that valued it at $1.414 trillion, and its shares fell about 9% Friday, their second day of trading, giving back much of Thursday’s 17% pop. Reuters cited worries about slower data-center expansion, higher borrowing costs and Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
The people with the most money in stocks already felt it. Those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances in the University of Michigan’s November survey, which ran through Nov. 16, “consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets,” survey director Joanne Hsu said.
What the panic looked like
Chipmakers took the worst of it. Micron, hotlink]Broadcom[/hotlink], Nvidia, and AMD were down between roughly 12% and 14%. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, topped 30 for the first time since March, CNBC reported.
The selling wasn’t only in the U.S. Taiwan’s stock index fell 5.65% Friday, capping its steepest weekly drop since October 1997, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC. Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell about 5%.
Washington added to it. President Donald Trump threatened a “tremendous tax” on U.S. companies that build data centers abroad, CNBC reported.
At midday, some analysts still saw a rotation.
“Money is leaving tech, not the market,” independent tech analyst Luke Lango, editor of the Innovation Investor newsletter, wrote in a note at 12:59 p.m. He said the Dow and the equal-weight S&P were higher at the time. His advice: Avoid AI stocks “while they’re being combative teenagers.” He also pointed to credit: SpaceX had to raise the yield on its $32 billion debt sale to 8.3%, which he read as the “capital spigot” closing for weaker AI borrowers such as CoreWeave and Nebius.
The calm-down chorus
Most of the Street said the drop would pass.
“Given the solid economic and fundamental backdrop, the move appears to be highly sentiment driven,” Chris Larkin, head of trading at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley, said in commentary sent to Fortune. He added that “only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983” turned into bear markets.
Deutsche Bank’s Binky Chadha called the market “very oversold” and said growth and earnings remained strong, according to CNBC. JPMorgan Asset Management chief global strategist David Kelly told Seeking Alpha markets were overdue for a tech correction. Chuck Carlson, CEO of Horizon Investment Services, told Reuters the market may be in a correction within a bull market.
E*Trade’s own research is less soothing. A March 2025 E*TRADE study of the 14 times since 1983 that the S&P 500 first closed 10% or more below a record found five became bear markets. But the index fell another 10% or more after closing in correction six of those 14 times, and in 1990 and 1998 it came within a point of bear territory. The median total drop from the record was 19.9%.
The backdrop Larkin calls solid includes a rate hike on the way. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday the central bank will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high, Reuters reported. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, per CME FedWatch, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.
The Fed meets Dec. 9. Investors will find out then whether Friday was panic or just early.

U.S. stocks fell sharply Friday as a deepening sell-off in artificial intelligence and technology shares pushed the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year and drove the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average into or near correction territory.

The S&P 500 slid roughly 3%, putting it more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record high and confirming a technical correction. The sell-off is a reflection of growing skepticism that the capital pouring into data centers, chips and AI models will generate the returns currently priced into stocks and the anti-AI sentiment of the incoming Democratic Congress with the prospect of new restrictions on data-center construction.
More than $1 trillion in S&P 500 market value alone was wiped out on Friday. Global equities have lost nearly $9 trillion in market value since their August peak. Bloomberg has documented a $750-plus billion web of AI financing where Nvidia invests in chip buyers, those buyers borrow to buy more chips, and the same capital loops back as reported revenue. sources.news_title: Three Reasons Why US Stock Markets Are Falling: Nasdaq Turns Negative For 2026, S&P Down 2%
After Anthropic Euphoria, Nvidia, AMD & the Broader Market Offer a Harsh Reality Check
sources.text:
The Week In Short
AMD faces down investor fears that its AI deals are looking a bit too intertwined with customers. Gary Marcus explains why he thinks the big AI companies are on shaky ground on the podcast.The first Nvidia earnings call post-Jensen Huang beat Wall Street expectations, but that wasn’t enough to rally the stock for long. Google’s new model Gemini 4 Neon proves wrong the critics who said it fell out of the AI race. Palo Alto Networks scoops up Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. Kalshi faces multiple investigations around whether or not it’s circumventing state gambling laws. The cyber outages continue to pile up. California and Arizona take action against OpenAI. European VCs push to establish their standing at Slush.
The Main Item
Circular Financing & China Worries Hit Nvidia Rival AMD as Markets Turn Against the AI Trade
It was remarkable to see Anthropic’s IPO plow through the various bits of worrying news that are piling up for the AI industry, with the core thesis of the investing mania very much intact.
The argument that chip companies investing in their customers is a dangerous form of circular financing akin to the telecom bubble of the early 2000s is very much intact too. And it’s not just Nvidia.
Hunterbrook, a short-seller that’s built an investigative journalism arm, said in a report entitled “Bank of AMD” that the number two player in AI chips has run an extensive customer-financing-and-investing operation that features “all of the circular financing of Nvidia, but without the margins or pricing power.” In a separate story, Hunterbrook said AMD has a China problem too, in the form of updated chip firmware being delivered to multiple blacklisted Chinese entities.
The news added fuel to a broad selloff in tech stocks that was hitting even newly public Anthropic on Friday.
Like Nvidia, AMD also sells lots of chips to Asian neoclouds that serve China’s big tech companies, and those revenues are at risk from new US government export control rules. AMD said the Hunterbrook reports didn’t properly represent its business, but shares fell almost 10% on the news. “If the smoke surrounding Nvidia becomes an inferno for the AI build-out, AMD will be engulfed by the flames,” Hunterbrook Capital said.
It’s of course helpful for Jensen Huang and Nvidia if AMD’s CEO, the widely respected Lisa Su, was doing some of the same things in pushing the envelope on deal-making and China sales (though no one is accusing her of improper personal conduct). But it’s decidedly not helpful for the startup ecosystem if another company that has been a major financier of the AI buildout has to slow or stop spending.
A lot of entities are getting cold feet about the bubbly extremes of the AI trade. Big Wall Street investment firms that promised in August to pony up some $500 billion in loans for data centers have yet to dispense a dime, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.
For months, investors have been waiting for the Anthropic IPO as the definitive validator of the industry and a counterpoint to all the talk about bubbles. It went off better than anyone could have expected. And yet, across the AI industry, a lot of people are selling on the news.
Broader markets took a beating Thursday — it was only Anthropic that soared, and maybe not for long. Investors and entrepreneurs won’t be breathing easy for quite a while yet.
Newcomer Podcast
Is OpenAI Becoming the WeWork of AI? | Gary Marcus 
Nvidia Woes
Nvidia’s Earnings Call Couldn’t Quell Doubts About its Post-Jensen Huang Future
Nvidia on Tuesday reported earnings that comfortably beat Wall Street expectations, with quarterly sales surpassing $100 billion for the first time. The figures were enough to rally the stock briefly, but it fell back Wednesday and closed down 3.3% at $146 Thursday. New board chair Harvey Jones didn’t sound like a replacement CEO was coming anytime soon and ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO following his forced resignation last week.
Chatter about a Huang comeback kicked up again after he said he’d be willing to return as CEO if the board asked, and three directors have privately pushed for him to be reinstated, per Semafor. Yet the gravity of the allegations relating to possible export control violations, to say nothing of affairs with a major customer and employees, makes a comeback unlikely.
Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner said the letter he sent the board Friday, widely seen as endorsing a Huang comeback, was not that, and he doesn’t want the board to “take shortcuts” in its investigation.
Ben Thompson at Stratechery, meanwhile, wrote an informal obituary for the Nvidia of old and doesn’t see how the company can hold onto its status post-Huang, given how crucial his relationships were with TSMC, neocloud customers, and the startups he backed.
The biggest immediate concern in startup land is interim CEO Colette Kress making it clear that she intends to dial back Huang’s aggressive dealmaking. Per data from Crunchbase, Nvidia and its venture arm, NVentures, have made a record 121 investments so far in 2026, with the pace of deals accelerating year by year since its 2023 base.
The Empire Strikes Back
Google Regains its Footing in the Frontier Model Competition
Amidst all the Anthropic hoopla, it was easy to miss a hugely important piece of news: Google has reestablished itself in the AI model race.
This week it released Gemini 4 Neon, a medium-sized model that had long been in the works. According to the benchmarks, Neon is ranking at or near the top of the most powerful models. And, maybe more importantly, it’s getting good reviews on X from the AI tastemakers who seem to have influence on how these models are adopted.
Google has struggled with its latest Gemini models. Gemini 3.5 Pro was delayed and its previous smaller models were not matching up with Anthropic and OpenAI (and even SpaceX). That kicked off an increasing sense within the AI world that Google was struggling — SemiAnalysis went as far as to flatly declare it cooked and out of the race. “DeepMind is no longer a frontier lab,” they wrote.
SemiAnalysis is a respected outfit when it comes to covering AI models and infrastructure, and kudos to them for going out on a limb with a bold declarative assessment. But it always rang hollow to anyone who has followed the progress of AI models. One of the recurring lessons of AI is that if a lab has the talent and the computing resources, it is never out of the mix. Certainly a lab can be waylaid by bad management and unsuccessful model runs, as DeepMind was, but to fully count them out doesn’t make sense. We’ve been here many times before: OpenAI after GPT-5, Anthropic after Opus 5, and xAI/SpaceX countless times. The individual moat for the frontier labs is far shallower than people like to think.
SemiAnalysis was humble about it and (now former) DeepMind leader Demis Hassabis was good natured in response. But a lesson learned? Probably not.

The three leaders agreed to collaborate on nuclear and energy issues but there was nothing concrete. Earlier in the week the US government announced broader restrictions on chips exports to selected high-risk countries, and we think despite the warm tone between the leaders in Shenzhen, China might still retaliate at some point.
During the week we adjusted our Fed and ECB calls adding an additional hike to each. We now expect the Fed to raise rates by 25bp at the next three meetings (December, January and March). This will bring the fed funds rate target range to 4.50-4.75%, where we expect it to remain for the rest of 2027. In the US, macro indicators continue to surprise us to the upside. We also see that the labour market is relatively tight and that inflation is broadening, especially in services, justifying an additional hike. In Europe, we now expect the ECB to hike in December and March bringing the deposit rate to 3.00% where it will remain for 2027. Recent comments from the ECB have been on the hawkish side with ECB members already starting to say that another hike in 2027 would not be unreasonable. We are also increasingly seeing spillovers from energy into core inflation with momentum rising.
Next week will bring plenty of interesting data releases. First up, on Monday S&P will release November PMIs for major economies. Over the past month, we have seen signs pointing to a cooling in the manufacturing cycle as economic surprise indices have edged lower, and the price of industrial metals have declined. On Wednesday the US PCE for October will be released. Retail energy prices have declined in the US from September to October which should ease some pressures on the headline m/m growth rate. On Thursday the ECB will publish minutes from the October meeting. We expect the minutes to confirm that a December hike is basically already a done deal.

sources.news_title: Markets plunge as Nasdaq erases gains for the year
sources.text:
The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks.
The dramatic sell off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year.
Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price.
Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant.
With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid-19 pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year.
The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%.
The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process.
While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weeks-long slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices, rising interest rates, mounting corporate debt loads, stubborn inflation, supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices.
The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China.
“The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.”

S&P 500 Falls 8.22% From October High as Klement Warns of AI Bubble
The index closed at 7,175 on Nov. 19, while remaining up 4.63% year to date.
The S&P 500 closed at 7,175 on Nov. 19, down 8.22% from 7,818 on Oct. 6, as Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement warned that his firm believes the artificial intelligence bubble is about to burst.
Klement, the firm’s Head of Strategy, Economics and ESG, said on Nov. 19 that he was selling stocks and moving to an entirely defensive position. He pointed to the index’s recent move below its 200-day moving average, while cautioning that the indicator is not foolproof.
The index was still up 4.63% year to date through the Nov. 19 close. The index had been declining for about a month and a half.

sources.news_title: Analyst warns ‘AI bubble is about to burst’ as S&P 500 plummets
sources.text:
As the June big tech highs started to grow more distant, the sentiment appeared to be shifting from excitement about the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and toward anxiety regarding the AI bubble.
Still, while multiple analysts warned of the looming danger, few have been ready to forecast a crisis. In October, Ed Yardeni revealed that the bubble indicators have become many, but that crash warnings remained few. By the start of November, professor and economist Steve Hanke warned of a major threat of a crisis, yet one with odds of happening lower than 50%.
By November 19, Panmure Liberum Head of Strategy, Economics, and ESG, Joachim Klement, broke the trend, explicitly stating that his firm thinks that ‘the AI bubble is about to burst’ and that he is selling his stocks.
Based on his writing, the watershed moment behind the decision to go entirely defensive came with the S&P 500 recently breaking its 200-day moving average (MA). Though Klement clarified that the indicator was not ‘foolproof’, he emphasized that the other market conditions also paint an exceedingly bearish picture.
Notably, though the benchmark index remains 4.63% in the green year-to-date (YTD), it has taken a downward turn a month and a half ago, crashing 8.22% from 7,818 on October 6 to 7,175 at the Thursday, November 19 close.
Why Wall Street remains bullish despite staring down an AI crash?
Curiously, Joachim Klement reflected on the ratings assigned by other prominent institutional analysts in a Reuters article published on November 18.
Indeed, he underlined that history shows that Wall Street experts tended to remain bullish regarding the stock market until the moment the crises started in earnest, with the Dot-com bubble representing a prime example.
Business Insider co-founder Henry Blodget was famously barred for life from working in the securities industry due to, in a nutshell, being highly optimistic about internet stocks publicly while privately expressing starkly bearish attitudes.
The 2003 case might be especially relevant in the context of the AI bubble since the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) removed some of the rules meant to prevent such behavior in late 2025, justifying the decision by claiming they had become superfluous.
Could the Anthropic stock IPO be the final nail in the AI trade?
Lastly, the latest events appear to lend credence to Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement bearish assessment. Following more than a month of decline and a series of scandals centered on one of the most important companies in the AI sector – Nvidia – Anthropic (NASDAQ: ANT) seemingly tried and failed to reignite confidence.
Indeed, the lab’s initial public offering (IPO) was expected by some to end the wider tech sell-off, but ANT shares hitting the market on November 19 were, nonetheless, accompanied by a steep and sweeping daily loss.
Furthermore, Anthropic itself appears to have made a round trip in less than 24 hours. ANT stock soared from its IPO price of $83, reaching highs above $110 and then, if the Friday, November 20 pre-market is included, plummeted toward $86 for an 11.36% extended-session crash.

sources.news_title: Today’s Market Movers: Anthropic, Nvidia, AMD, Intuit, Bloom Energy Under Pressure
sources.text:
TLDR
- Anthropic shares fell about 14% premarket after a record $81 billion IPO.
- AMD dropped after a short seller questioned its China ties.
- Nvidia is on track for a seventh straight losing day.
- Intuit fell about 9.9% on a weak outlook and a Mailchimp sale.
- Ross Stores and BJ’s Wholesale fell, while Gap gained.
US stock futures fell on Friday, November 20, as the sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks deepened. Investors also reacted to weak guidance from Intuit and several large retailers.
Technology names including Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices extended recent losses. Here is how the biggest movers traded before the opening bell.
Anthropic Slips After Record Debut
Anthropic shares fell about 14% in premarket trading. The drop gave back much of the gain from Thursday’s first day as a public company.
The Claude developer completed the largest IPO in history. It raised about $81 billion after pricing shares at $83.
The stock jumped to $111.50 on Thursday before closing at $97.17. That close was about 17% above the offering price.
A 14% drop from that close would put shares near the $83 offering price. Reuters reported that the move added to concerns about AI valuations and the heavy spending needed to build advanced models.
Chip Stocks, Software and Retailers Also Slide
Advanced Micro Devices fell about 6.8% in premarket trading after dropping 7.7% on Thursday. The decline followed a report from short seller Hunterbrook Capital.
The report questioned the chipmaker’s ties to Chinese technology firms. It pointed to IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker that faces US export limits.
AMD rejected the claims and said the report misrepresented its business. The company says it follows US export-control rules.
Nvidia shares dropped about 3.8%, which puts the stock on track for a seventh straight losing day. The fall came even though the company reported strong earnings earlier this week, and Barron’s said shares are well below their October peak.
Bloom Energy fell about 8% and Sandisk dropped 8.1%. Coherent, Corning, Dell, Intel, Marvell, Micron, Seagate and Western Digital also traded lower.
Intuit shares fell about 9.9%, making the company one of the biggest premarket losers in the S&P 500. It gave a disappointing revenue outlook to investors.
Intuit also plans to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, according to its announcement. It bought the email marketing platform for about $12 billion in 2021.
Gap rose about 3% after reporting third-quarter adjusted earnings of $0.82 per share, above expectations. The retailer cut its full-year sales and profit forecasts.
Ross Stores fell about 6.3% despite solid quarterly results. Its cautious holiday-quarter outlook weighed on the shares.
BJ’s Wholesale Club dropped about 6% after earnings that included a $240 million benefit from a legal settlement. The one-time gain raised questions about underlying profit.
Bill Holdings fell about 3.7% after TPG and Corpay agreed to take the company private. The deal values it at about $6 billion, or $63.25 per share in cash.

sources.news_title: S&P 500 drops 3.7% as Nasdaq turns negative for 2026
sources.text:
(AP) — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period.
SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.
